The digital courthouse may be open—yet ordinary people can still be left on the steps.

Court administrators may answer that records remain available through clerk offices or limited search portals. That claim doesn't resolve the problem. A paper index (the old card catalog) and a searchable database are not equivalent forms of access. Researchers, journalists, tenants, small businesses, and families may need to trace a case across names, dates, and related filings (not merely retrieve one known document). When private services provide that practical capacity while public systems can't, money determines who can see the law operating.

What does “public” mean if meaningful search is reserved for institutions that can absorb recurring fees? It should mean more than permission to inspect a document after supplying the exact court, case number, and filing date (details many users do not have). A record that can be found only by someone who already knows where it is isn't meaningfully discoverable. The difference matters because judicial decisions affect liberty, property, family relationships, and government power—not just the professional routines of lawyers.

Private database companies can offer useful tools, and specialized services may justify specialized prices. That concession does not require surrendering the public foundation. Courts should provide a reliable baseline: searchable dockets, opinions, filed documents subject to lawful restrictions, stable links, and downloads in common formats (including formats accessible to people using assistive technology). Vendors can compete above that floor—with advanced analytics, alerts, or workflow features—without charging admission to the underlying civic record.

Privacy requires equal seriousness. Broad digital availability may expose sensitive information more rapidly than a trip to a courthouse would, and some records must be sealed or redacted (for example, protected personal identifiers). Courts are moving records from courthouse counters to online systems, a change advertised as faster and more convenient. But convenience isn't public access when the usable doorway belongs to an expensive private database. If opinions, dockets, and filings are public in principle but difficult to find without a costly subscription, the public right has been preserved on paper and narrowed in practice. The digital courthouse may be open—yet ordinary people can still be left on the steps.

Court administrators may answer that records remain available through clerk offices or limited search portals. That claim doesn't resolve the problem. A paper index (the old card catalog) and a searchable database are not equivalent forms of access. Researchers, journalists, tenants, small businesses, and families may need to trace a case across names, dates, and related filings (not merely retrieve one known document). When private services provide that practical capacity while public systems can't, money determines who can see the law operating.

What does “public” mean if meaningful search is reserved for institutions that can absorb recurring fees? It should mean more than permission to inspect a document after supplying the exact court, case number, and filing date (details many users do not have). A record that can be found only by someone who already knows where it is isn't meaningfully discoverable. The difference matters because judicial decisions affect liberty, property, family relationships, and government power—not just the professional routines of lawyers.

Private database companies can offer useful tools, and specialized services may justify specialized prices. That concession does not require surrendering the public foundation. Courts should provide a reliable baseline: searchable dockets, opinions, filed documents subject to lawful restrictions, stable links, and downloads in common formats (including formats accessible to people using assistive technology). Vendors can compete above that floor—with advanced analytics, alerts, or workflow features—without charging admission to the underlying civic record.

Privacy requires equal seriousness. Broad digital availability may expose sensitive information more rapidly than a trip to a courthouse would, and some records must be sealed or redacted (for example, protected personal identifiers). But privacy isn't protected by making comprehensive access affordable only to wealthy subscribers. That arrangement creates a vault with two keys: one costly and efficient, the other nominally free but cumbersome. The answer is careful access rules (including meaningful redaction and review), not a price barrier that favors powerful users.

Funding is a real concern. Building secure, usable systems costs money, and courts shouldn't be asked to maintain them with slogans. Legislatures can appropriate funds, courts can adopt reasonable copying charges for exceptional services, and agencies can publish open technical standards (so records aren't trapped in one vendor's format). What they should not do is convert a constitutional institution's public output into a commercial bottleneck. Cost may explain a weak portal; it is not a sufficient defense of unequal access.

The practical test is simple. If you receive a court notice, investigate official conduct, or try to understand a case affecting your community, can you find the relevant public materials without buying professional access? We believe the answer must be yes. Our courts exercise public power, and their records should remain genuinely public—searchable, usable, affordable, and protected by sensible privacy rules. Lawmakers and court administrators must fund that baseline, require open formats, and refuse contracts that make a private subscription the price of seeing public justice.
